headline: A 12MB Go Binary That Hands AI Agents the Browser
lede: Browser automation has long been AI agents' clumsiest limb — screenshot-heavy, framework-locked, and expensive in tokens. PinchTab, an open-source Go binary, tries to fix all three at once by acting as a plain HTTP server that any agent, in any language, can drive with nothing more than curl. The pitch is deliberate simplicity: one file, one Chrome instance, and an API thin enough to read on a napkin.
body:
The core insight is that the dominant pattern — taking a screenshot of a web page and feeding it to a vision model — is wildly wasteful. A screenshot encodes every pixel of a rendered page; a vision model then has to infer structure from that image, typically at a cost of around 10,000 tokens per page. PinchTab takes a different path, parsing the **accessibility tree** instead. The *accessibility tree* is the same semantic structure that screen readers use to navigate a page: it describes interactive elements, their labels, and their relationships, without encoding any visual data. The result is a far leaner representation.

PinchTab exposes this tree, along with click, type, scroll, and navigation primitives, through a small set of HTTP endpoints. An agent navigates to a URL with a POST, fetches a snapshot with a GET, and acts on an element by referencing a stable shorthand — `e5`, say — rather than a brittle CSS selector or a pixel coordinate. The architecture is described as "one binary, one Chrome, HTTP in, CDP out" — CDP being the *Chrome DevTools Protocol*, the low-level interface Chrome exposes for programmatic control. There is no SDK to install, no Node runtime to manage, no Python environment to version-pin.

The stealth features are notable for a tool of this scope. PinchTab patches `navigator.webdriver`, spoofs the user agent, and strips other automation flags that major sites use to detect and block headless browsers. Persistent sessions mean cookies and authentication survive restarts, so a human can complete a two-factor login once and hand control to an agent for subsequent runs. A real-time dashboard handles multi-instance orchestration — several Chrome sessions running in parallel under one binary.

At the time of the post, the project had roughly 1,600 GitHub stars, 478 commits, and 15 releases, suggesting a codebase that has been actively shaped rather than thrown over the wall. It carries an MIT licence. Current version is v0.7.6. The comparison to Playwright MCP and other framework-tied tools is fair in that those solutions are designed as extensions of specific agent ecosystems; PinchTab is deliberately orthogonal — it cares only that its HTTP server is reachable.

concepts.definition: A structured, semantic representation of a web page's content and interactive elements, built by the browser for assistive technologies like screen readers. Unlike a screenshot, it describes what elements are present and what they do rather than how they look, making it far more compact for machine consumption.

A low-level protocol that Chrome and Chromium expose for programmatic inspection and control — navigating pages, reading the DOM, executing JavaScript, and capturing screenshots. Tools like Playwright, Puppeteer, and PinchTab all communicate with Chrome via CDP under the hood.

A set of patches applied to a headless browser session to disguise the fact that it is automated. Common techniques include overwriting the `navigator.webdriver` property, spoofing the user-agent string, and removing other signals that bot-detection services check for.

In the context of large language models, the cost of representing a given piece of information as input. Vision-based page snapshots are token-expensive because every pixel must be encoded; text-based accessibility trees are far leaner, reducing both latency and the dollar cost of each agent action.

repos.summary: PinchTab is a self-contained Go binary that launches a Chrome instance and exposes browser control through a plain HTTP API. Agents of any language can navigate pages, click elements, extract text, and manage multiple sessions without installing a framework. It uses the browser's accessibility tree rather than screenshots to keep token usage low.

fact_check: The tweet states that a full page snapshot via the `/text` endpoint costs '~800 tokens,' but PinchTab's own documentation benchmarks the tool at roughly 3,000 tokens without prior context and over 1,000 tokens with context — both higher than the figure cited. The directional claim (substantially cheaper than a 10,000-token screenshot) holds up; the specific 800-token number appears optimistic. The tweet also refers to 'OpenClaw's browser' as a framework-locked competitor, but no product by that name appears in the research sources or in PinchTab's documentation. The name may be a satirical stand-in for another tool; the claim cannot be verified as written.
